source_title: Rivian Automotive, Inc. Form 10-K for fiscal year ended December 31, 2023
publisher_issuer: Rivian Automotive, Inc. (filed with U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission); full-year 2023 figures corroborated by Rivian Q4/FY2023 earnings release and Reuters/CNBC-class reporting
company_context: Rivian is a US electric-vehicle manufacturer (R1T pickup, R1S SUV, and commercial vans). In fiscal 2023 it scaled production sharply while still consuming large amounts of cash per vehicle, a classic high-revenue-ramp-with-heavy-burn profile typical of capital-intensive manufacturing scale-up.
business_type: Capital-intensive EV manufacturing and direct sales; large fixed-cost plant ramp with negative unit economics during scale-up
company_size_stage: large-cap public, early commercial-scale manufacturer (pre-profitability ramp)
geography: United States (primary manufacturing in Normal, Illinois)
macro_context: Post-2022 EV demand softening, high interest rates raising the cost of capital for cash-burning growth companies, and intense EV price competition led by Tesla price cuts.
outcome_category: 7 - high revenue but cash crisis / heavy burn
evidence_summary: Rivian grew 2023 revenue to about $4.43 billion (up roughly 167% from $1.66 billion in 2022) and produced 57,232 vehicles while delivering 50,122, beating its own raised production guidance. Despite the revenue ramp, the company posted a net loss of about $5.43 billion and used roughly $4.87 billion of cash in operating activities, ending 2023 with about $7.86 billion in cash and cash equivalents (about $9.37 billion including short-term investments, and about $10.47 billion of total liquidity including the revolving credit facility). This is the canonical high-revenue, high-burn manufacturing scale-up where the binding constraint is cash runway and operational cost-down rather than top-line demand alone.
owner_decision_context: Management chose to keep scaling production capacity and a high cost base ahead of profitability, betting that volume ramp and cost-down would outrun the cash burn while preserving multi-year runway via large cash reserves.
action_taken: Continued aggressive production ramp and plant investment while consuming roughly $4.9 billion of operating cash in the year; relied on a large existing cash balance plus a revolving credit facility for runway rather than an emergency raise.
outcome_evidence: Year-end liquidity of about $9.37 billion (about $10.47 billion including revolver) against roughly $4.87 billion annual operating cash burn documents a multi-quarter but finite runway, defining the case as a high-revenue cash-management problem rather than a demand collapse.
source_limitations: WebFetch of sec.gov returns HTTP 403 in this environment; figures are verified from the FY2023 10-K / Q4-FY2023 earnings release as reported verbatim in search snippets from primary (sec.gov, Rivian) and credible secondary domains, not from full-text read of the filing. Operating cash burn and revenue are GAAP; total-liquidity figure includes undrawn revolver capacity.

inferred: At roughly $4.9 billion annual operating burn, the binding constraint is cash runway and per-unit cost-down, not aggregate demand
The case is an operational-cost-and-liquidity problem (scale-up economics) rather than a solvency or demand-collapse event
why_useful_for_opsiq: Clean outcome-7 high-revenue / heavy-burn manufacturing case with audited SEC figures. Tests whether OpsIQ recognizes a cash_liquidity_crisis and operational_bottleneck (cost-down / throughput) profile in a growing company, rather than mislabeling strong revenue growth as health. Strong for runway-aware adaptive re-evaluation and capex-risk modeling.
